title: Why AI has a weird attention span you must learn to manage · hancrafted
description: AI's attention span, its context window, is a limited resource you have to actively manage: one chat per job, a handoff after real progress or before a break, and for bigger projects one planner chat that hands each step to a fresh chat.

S Sister Call · 1:21:40 Summer party Chat with AI · one hour Let's sort out the holidays! Yes! But first, did you hear about Mum’s new phone? The start Plan a summer party for our team: 40 people, end of June, budget 40,000 euro . Happy to help! Indoor or outdoor? Any dietary needs I should know about? She sent me forty photos of her thumb. Ha! Did you see the neighbours’ renovation? Don’t get me started. And my back hurts again. The middle Find three venues in Lisbon. Fetched 10 pages · 15k of extracts Three options: Quinta terrace, LX Factory rooftop, Estrela garden pavilion. The catering offers are in the project folder. Which one fits? Read catering-offers.pdf · 20 pages Check hotels near the venue for 15 guests from abroad. Hotel Lumen and Casa do Rio both have 15 rooms free on 27 June. And Pepper ate a whole birthday cake, candles included! The standout Got it: 40 guests, 15 travelling, 12 vegetarian . Said four times, so a fresh copy is always near the end. Not yet. Oh, dinner is ready, I have to run. Talk soon, bye! The end Great, put the full plan together. Full plan: venue 14,800 , catering with the vegetarian menu 21,600 , hotels 9,400 , music 6,500 . Total 52,300 euro . 12,300 over the budget from the first message With your sister, a lost detail is funny. With a deadline, it’s expensive. The long phone call Recall is U-shaped In free recall of a word list, the first and last items are recalled best and the middle ones worst 1 . Sources (1) Murdock, The serial position effect of free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Why the start sticks People rehearse early items more often than middle ones, and the number of rehearsals predicts recall 1 . Sources (1) Rundus, Analysis of rehearsal processes in free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Why the end sticks Delaying recall with a distractor task removes the recency part but leaves the start intact, which points to two separate stores 1 ; where recency comes from is still debated 2 . Sources (2) Glanzer and Cunitz, Two storage mechanisms in free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Bjork and Whitten, Recency-sensitive retrieval processes in long-term free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org The standout survives An item that differs from its neighbours is remembered better, and it stands out against its context, not on its own 1 2 . Sources (2) von Restorff, Über die Wirkung von Bereichsbildungen im Spurenfeld ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Hunt, The subtlety of distinctiveness: What von Restorff really did ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Lab lists, not phone calls Every study uses word lists or short material, so that the same pattern holds for an hour-long call is an inference, though the effects are textbook findings 1 . Sources (1) Murdock, The serial position effect of free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org

AI forgets the middle too Measured, even for long-input models Relevant information is used best at the beginning or end of the input and worst in the middle, also in models built for long contexts 1 . Sources (1) Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org A built-in pull to the start The first tokens of an input draw strong attention as an "attention sink", even when they carry no meaning 1 . Sources (1) Xiao et al., Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Two position effects Causal masking biases attention toward earlier positions, and relative position encodings favour nearby tokens, which trades off against the accumulating importance of early positions 1 ; that these two together produce the middle dip is an inference, the paper's abstract does not state it. Sources (1) Wu et al., On the Emergence of Position Bias in Transformers ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org The strength varies The dip is strongest when the input fills up to about half the window; beyond that the start advantage fades and the end advantage stays 1 . Sources (1) Veseli et al., Positional Biases Shift as Inputs Approach Context Window Limits ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Planted facts, not chat products The studies plant a fact in the input and test whether the model retrieves it; none tests current chat products, so applying them to a chat is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

The long phone call 0:00 – 0:33 A long chat is a long call Imagine the last long phone call you had with someone close, a sister, a friend, your mum. You called to settle one thing, and an hour later you hung up. Before I say a word about AI, I want you to feel what that call left you with, because the question I want to ask you is whether a long AI chat does the same thing to you, so the call comes first and the chat second.

The long phone call 0:00 – 0:18 The start sticks Say you call your sister to sort out the holidays. "Let's sort out the holidays!" is how it starts, and that first line sets the frame for everything after it, so you still remember it at the end. That is called primacy. 0:18 – 0:30 The end sticks You also remember how it ended. "Talk soon, bye", and the last few minutes before it, because they just happened and are still fresh. That is called recency. 0:30 – 0:48 The middle blurs Now the middle. An hour of detail went by, the neighbours' renovation, Mum's new phone, your sister's back pain, and if someone asked you what was in it, you could hardly say. All of it was said, and very little of it stayed. 0:48 – 1:05 One thing stands out Except one thing. Pepper ate a whole birthday cake, candles included. Nobody asked you to keep that, and you can still tell it, because what is different from everything around it survives. That is called the isolation effect. 1:05 – 1:24 We never fixed the date And then the punchline. Dinner is ready, she has to run, and you realise: we never fixed the date. The one thing you called for never got settled. (pause) Hold on to that, because the question is whether an AI chat does the same.

AI forgets the middle too 0:00 – 0:26 Meet the summer-party chat So let me introduce a chat that stays with us for the rest of the episode. You plan a company summer party with an AI: 40 people, end of June, a budget of 40,000 euro, and you give it a catering PDF and a guest list. Remember this chat, because we come back to it on every slide that follows. 0:26 – 0:56 It happens in a long chat too Now let it run for an hour. You started with the plan and the budget, and the first messages tend to get used, the latest messages tend to get used, and the middle gets lost. A detail you keep repeating, like the 12 vegetarian guests, survives. Later the budget slips, which is odd for a number from your very first message, and why that happens comes on a later slide. 0:56 – 1:16 A shape, not a brain I'm not saying the AI thinks the way you do. It has no sister and no Mum with a new phone. What I'm saying is that the shape is the same, and a shape is something you can predict, so you know where to expect the slip. 1:16 – 1:32 What a lost detail costs With your sister, a lost detail is funny. With a deadline, it's expensive. So ask yourself which one your chat is: the one with the dog and the cake, or the one with your budget in it.

The AI's attention span 0:00 – 0:17 Why it happens So far you have seen what happens. Now the cause, because once you know how the AI holds a chat, the pattern stops being a surprise, and only after that do we look at what it does to your answers.

What fills the window 0:00 – 0:13 More in there than you typed You have seen the window fill with your messages. But your messages are only a part of it, so the next question is what else goes in without you noticing.
Managing the attention span 0:00 – 0:09 You manage by habit You can't read a gauge, so you build habits. First the everyday ones, and then the one for a big project.
